n: Job continues: if God sets times for judgment, why don’t his faithful ever get to see those days of justice? He is troubled by how long evil goes unpunished.
Job describes oppressors: they move boundary stones to steal land and seize flocks to graze as their own.

f.g: Moving boundary stones to steal a neighbor’s land — a serious crime in Israel’s law.

n: They take an orphan’s only donkey and seize a widow’s ox as collateral, leaving them helpless.

f.w: the widow's ox for a pledge

n: They push the needy off the road, and the poor have to hide together for safety.

f.w: turn the needy out of the way

n: The poor are forced to live like wild donkeys in the desert, rising early to scrounge for food for their children.
They glean leftovers in other people’s fields and pick the last grapes in the vineyards of the wicked.

f.g: Grain in general, not American maize.

n: Stripped of their clothes, they spend nights in the cold with nothing to cover them.
They are soaked by mountain rains and cling to the rocks for shelter.

f.g: Huddle against rocks with no other shelter.

n: The oppressors even snatch a fatherless baby from its mother and take a poor person’s child as collateral for a debt.

f.w: pluck the fatherless from the breast

n: The poor go about without clothes and carry grain for others while they themselves go hungry.

f.w: take away the sheaf from the hungry
f.g: Better “though hungry, they carry the sheaves” for their masters.

n: They press olives and tread grapes for others, yet go thirsty themselves.

f.g: Crushing grapes with bare feet in a stone vat.

n: In the city the dying groan and the wounded cry for help — yet God does not seem to charge anyone with wrong. This is Job’s honest anguish.

f.g: Does not hold anyone accountable — or “pays no attention to their prayer.”

n: Job now turns to people who rebel against light — those who love darkness because their deeds are evil.
The murderer gets up at dawn to kill the poor, and at night he prowls like a thief.
The adulterer waits for dusk, thinking no one sees, and hides his face.
Thieves break into houses in the dark after marking them during the day. They avoid the light.

f.g: Break through mud-brick walls to steal.

n: For such people, morning is as frightening as deep darkness is for others; they are at home with night’s terrors.
Verses 18–24 may describe what the friends say happens to the wicked, or what Job hopes will happen: they are swept away like foam on water and their land is cursed.

f.g: Quickly carried off by flood, like debris on water.

n: As drought and heat dry up melted snow, so the grave swallows sinners.
Even the mother who bore him forgets him; worms feast on him; wickedness is broken like a tree.

f.w: the worm shall feed sweetly on him

n: He mistreats the childless woman and does nothing good for the widow.

f.g: A woman without children, who had no one to support her.

f.w: doeth not good to the widow

n: Yet God, by his power, prolongs the life of the mighty; they rise up even when they despair of living.

f.w: no man is sure of life
f.g: He rises even when he has given up hope of life.

n: God lets them feel secure, yet his eyes are on all their ways. Nothing escapes him.

f.w: his eyes are upon their ways

n: They are exalted for a short time, then brought low and cut off like heads of grain at harvest.

f.w: cut off as the tops of the ears of corn

n: Job challenges anyone to prove him wrong about what he has seen. His observations stand.

f.w: who will make me a liar
f.g: Who can show my words to be false?
